title: There's a restraint order from admission
objective: Use restraint only after less restrictive measures fail, on a time-limited order that is never PRN, with ongoing monitoring
secondaryObjectives: Apply safety protocols for skin, falls, restraint, hourly rounding and suicide risk
Recognize patient, drug, environment and equipment risk factors for harm

sources.cite: Jaqua EE, Nguyen VTN, Chin E. Delirium in older persons: prevention, evaluation, and management. Am Fam Physician 2023;108(3):278-287
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes. Delirium is an 'acute disturbance in attention, cognition, and awareness that fluctuates over time'; precipitants include 'Urinary or stool retention', 'Uncontrolled pain' and 'Infection'; nonpharmacologic measures are 'the foundation of delirium management and prevention'; 'Physical restraints should be avoided because they have been correlated with worse outcomes', used only after other options are exhausted; medication only when conservative treatment fails and agitation is severe.
Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

brief.situation: 02:10 on an orthopedic med-surg unit. You are Mrs. Abbott's nurse. She is 81, two days after repair of a hip fracture, and normally lives alone and manages her own affairs. Tonight she is pulling at her IV, calling for her late husband and trying to climb over the bed rail.
handover: Evening: oriented and pleasant. Last urine recorded at 17:00. Oxycodone at 20:00 for hip pain.
The night supervisor passing by: 'There's a PRN soft wrist restraint order from admission. Put them on and she'll settle.'

Unit protocols: a bladder scan and straight catheter for retention over 600 mL; low bed, bed alarm and a sitter on request; the covering provider by phone. The unit's restraint policy follows federal rules.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what is driving her behavior and what keeps her safe.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Agitation from a full bladder climbs toward an attempt to get out of bed. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Agitation settles once the bladder is emptied and she is reoriented. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point at which she climbs out of bed. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Minutes in wrist restraints before the struggle injures her (authored: 8). FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Fall precautions in place within 10 minutes (unit practice).
The covering provider reviews by phone and comes to the bedside: about 20 min.

why.question: Should Mrs. Abbott go into wrist restraints under the order from admission?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention after hip surgery is delirium; a bladder of 840 mL with nothing voided since 17:00 and hip pain are precipitants to treat.
parts.modelAnswer: No. This is new delirium, and it has a cause: her bladder holds 840 mL and she hasn't voided since 17:00, plus her hip hurts. Treating those will settle her more than any restraint.

parts.label: Restraint and the order
parts.criteria: Restraint only after less restrictive measures fail; a PRN restraint order is never valid; less restrictive measures first (catheter, low bed and alarm, sitter, reorientation, covering the IV); if restraint becomes unavoidable, a new time-limited order and ongoing monitoring.
parts.modelAnswer: A PRN restraint order isn't valid, and restraint comes only after less restrictive measures fail. I drain her bladder, treat her pain, put the bed low with the alarm, get a sitter, reorient her and cover the IV. If restraint ever became unavoidable, it would need a new time-limited order and close monitoring.

noProgress.rationale: Untreated delirium with nothing in place an hour on is harm here.

expertPath.text: Low bed, mats and alarm now; ask for a sitter. Don't apply the PRN restraint.
Delirium screen: positive. Pain and basics. Bladder scan: 840 mL.
Straight catheter by protocol; glasses, hearing aids, reorientation; cover the IV.
Report to the provider, including that the PRN restraint order isn't valid. Document.

restraintInjury.headline: Injured in restraints
restraintInjury.body: A PRN restraint order is never valid, and restraint comes only after less restrictive measures fail. Restraints are linked to worse outcomes in delirium.

fall.headline: A fall
fall.body: Put the low bed, alarm and a sitter in place early, and look for the cause: retention and pain are common precipitants of delirium.

settled.headline: Cause treated, no restraint
settled.body: You screened for delirium, found and drained the retention, kept her safe with less restrictive measures and refused an invalid order. That is the expert path.

settledGaps.headline: Settled, with gaps
settledGaps.body: Check when the bladder was scanned, when the fall precautions went in and whether delirium was screened.

time_up.headline: Still agitated
time_up.body: Look for the cause of delirium within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention after hip surgery is delirium, and a bladder of 840 mL with nothing voided since 17:00 is a precipitant to treat now. Restraint is used only after less restrictive measures fail, and a PRN restraint order is never valid; restraints are linked to worse outcomes in delirium. So: low bed, mats and alarm, a sitter, a straight catheter by protocol, pain addressed, glasses and hearing aids with reorientation, the IV covered, and a report to the provider.
